lessons.title: 6.1.1 What Is Career Development?
Content: Career development is the continuous process of understanding yourself, exploring professional opportunities, developing relevant capabilities, communicating your value, accessing work opportunities and progressing toward meaningful professional goals.
It involves more than getting a job.
- identifying the skills employers or clients need;
- preparing a professional CV and profile;
A person may be employed but still lack a career development strategy.
Another person may be unemployed but actively building skills, practical experience, a portfolio and professional relationships that improve their future opportunities.
The objective is to move from depending entirely on circumstances to taking deliberate responsibility for your professional development.
Do not merely search for work. Develop the capabilities, evidence and relationships that help you access, perform and progress in meaningful work.

lessons.title: 6.2.1 What Is the Labour Market?
Content: The labour market is the environment in which people offer their skills and services while employers, clients and organizations seek people who can perform particular kinds of work.
The labour market changes as technology, consumer needs, economic conditions, regulations and business models change.
A career decision should therefore consider both personal suitability and the demand for particular capabilities.
The Four Questions of Labour-Market Awareness
Identify occupations, industries, job functions and professional services.
Understand the needs that employers and clients are willing and able to pay people to address.
Identify the qualifications, skills, experience and professional standards associated with the work.
4. How can I demonstrate my ability?
Determine what evidence could establish that you can perform the work.

lessons.title: 6.2.2 Understanding Industries, Occupations and Job Titles
Content: These terms are related but different.
An industry is a broad area of economic activity.
An occupation is a type of work performed by people with related responsibilities or skills.
A job title is the name an employer gives to a particular position.
Job titles can differ between employers even when the underlying work is similar.
Therefore, students should examine job responsibilities and required capabilities rather than relying on titles alone.

lessons.title: 6.2.3 The Four Main Career Pathways
Content: A person does not need to follow only one employment model throughout life.
You work for an employer in exchange for compensation.
Your success depends on factors including competence, performance, professional conduct and the employer's needs.
You provide services to clients, often on a project or contract basis.
You must develop both the technical skill and the ability to attract clients, manage projects and deliver work.
You create and develop a business that provides products or services.
You may initially perform the work yourself before building a team or operational system.
You develop specialized expertise and provide professional services, subject to the relevant legal, licensing and qualification requirements.
Examples include certain engineering, legal, accounting and healthcare services.
Some people combine these pathways over time.
For example, a professional may be employed while building a portfolio, later begin freelancing and eventually establish a company.
Identify which pathway or combination of pathways best fits your current circumstances.

blocks.content:
A person does not need to follow only one employment model throughout life.

PATHWAY 1: EMPLOYMENT

You work for an employer in exchange for compensation.

Examples:

- administrative officer;

- engineer;

- accountant;

- teacher;

- operations manager.

Your success depends on factors including competence, performance, professional conduct and the employer's needs.

PATHWAY 2: FREELANCING

You provide services to clients, often on a project or contract basis.

Examples:

- graphic design;

- writing;

- website development;

- virtual assistance;

- video editing;

- bookkeeping.

You must develop both the technical skill and the ability to attract clients, manage projects and deliver work.

PATHWAY 3: ENTREPRENEURSHIP

You create and develop a business that provides products or services.

You may initially perform the work yourself before building a team or operational system.

PATHWAY 4: PROFESSIONAL OR TECHNICAL PRACTICE

You develop specialized expertise and provide professional services, subject to the relevant legal, licensing and qualification requirements.

Examples include certain engineering, legal, accounting and healthcare services.

Some people combine these pathways over time.

For example, a professional may be employed while building a portfolio, later begin freelancing and eventually establish a company.

Practical Exercise

Identify which pathway or combination of pathways best fits your current circumstances.

lessons.title: 6.3.2 The Difference Between Interest, Talent, Skill and Competence
Content: Something you enjoy or want to explore.
A natural or developed aptitude that may help you learn or perform an activity.
An ability developed through learning and practice.
The ability to apply relevant knowledge and skills to perform a task to an appropriate standard.
For example, a person may enjoy technology but lack programming skills.
After training and practice, the person may develop coding skills.
After completing projects and demonstrating that the work meets appropriate requirements, the person may have evidence of competence.
Interest may start the journey, but competence and evidence help demonstrate professional readiness.

lessons.title: 6.4.1 What Is Employability?
Content: Employability is the combination of capabilities, evidence, behaviours and adaptability that helps a person access work, perform effectively and develop professionally.
Employability is not simply having a certificate.
Different occupations require different combinations of these capabilities.
An electrician, accountant, software developer and customer support specialist do not need identical technical skills.
However, all may benefit from clear communication, reliability, problem-solving and the ability to learn.

lessons.title: 6.4.2 The SGG Employability Formula
Content: Use this as a learning framework:
EMPLOYABILITY = RELEVANT CAPABILITY + EVIDENCE + PROFESSIONAL BEHAVIOUR + OPPORTUNITY ACCESS + CONTINUOUS DEVELOPMENT
Can people work with you reliably and respectfully?
Can you identify and pursue relevant openings?
Can you improve as the role and market change?
This is a conceptual framework, not a scientifically calculated equation.

lessons.title: 6.5.1 Do Not Depend on Certificates Alone
Content: Certificates may provide evidence of training or assessment, depending on the issuing institution and credential.
They do not automatically prove that you can perform every task associated with a job.
Therefore, students should build evidence of ability alongside learning credentials.

blocks.content:
STEP 1: LEARN

Acquire the knowledge.

STEP 2: PRACTISE

Apply the knowledge to a task.

STEP 3: DEMONSTRATE

Produce evidence of your ability.

STEP 4: RECEIVE FEEDBACK

Identify errors and gaps.

STEP 5: IMPROVE

Correct the gaps and repeat the process.

STEP 6: DOCUMENT

Record the completed work and your contribution.

This cycle can be applied to almost any skill.

For example, a student learning spreadsheet analysis can:

1. learn spreadsheet fundamentals;

2. practise with sample data;

3. produce a useful report;

4. check the formulas;

5. improve the analysis;

6. save the final report as a portfolio sample.

The project demonstrates practical learning more clearly than simply claiming to have watched a course.

lessons.title: 6.5.3 Build a Career Portfolio
Content: A portfolio is a collection of evidence demonstrating your capabilities.
Depending on the occupation, it may contain:
For work involving confidential information, proprietary materials or client data, use only materials you are authorized to disclose. Where necessary, create anonymized or simulated examples.
A person without formal employment experience can build a portfolio using realistic practice projects.
Aspiring data analyst: Analyse a public dataset and prepare a report.
Aspiring graphic designer: Create a series of original sample designs.
Aspiring administrative assistant: Develop a sample filing system, meeting agenda and project tracker.
Aspiring software developer: Build a small application and document how it works.
Aspiring electrical technician: Document appropriate training exercises or projects within their competence and applicable safety requirements.
Aspiring business development professional: Prepare a sample market research report and outreach plan.
Show what you can do, explain how you did it and identify the value of the result.

lessons.title: 6.6.1 What Is a CV?
Content: A curriculum vitae (CV) is a document presenting relevant information about your education, experience, skills, achievements and qualifications.
In some countries and industries, the term CV refers to a relatively concise job-application document. In others, it may refer to a longer academic or professional record.
Always follow the employer's requested format and the conventions of the relevant market.
A CV is not your entire life story.
It is a professional document designed to help a reader assess your suitability for a particular opportunity.

lessons.title: 6.6.3 Standard CV Structure
Content: A general employment CV may contain the following sections.
Avoid including unnecessary sensitive personal information.
State your professional direction or area of expertise.
Entry-Level Customer Support Professional | Communication | Customer Service
Use a headline that reflects your actual capabilities.
Write a short summary of your relevant skills, experience and career direction.

«Entry-level administrative professional with experience organizing information, preparing documents and supporting routine office activities. Developing proficiency in digital productivity tools, professional communication and task coordination. Seeking an opportunity to contribute to an administrative or operations team while continuing to build practical competence.»
Do not copy this summary without adapting it to your real circumstances.
List relevant skills that you can reasonably demonstrate.
Separate technical skills from transferable skills when doing so improves readability.
Include relevant employment, contract work, internships, volunteering and other legitimate experience.
Describe your actual responsibilities and contributions.
Include relevant projects where formal employment experience is limited.
List relevant qualifications and institutions accurately.
Include relevant credentials with accurate titles and issuing organizations.
Include language proficiency, relevant professional memberships or other role-related information when appropriate.

blocks.content:
A general employment CV may contain the following sections.

1. Contact Information

Include appropriate professional contact details.

Examples:

- name;

- telephone number;

- professional email;

- city and country;

- LinkedIn profile, if relevant;

- portfolio link, if relevant.

Avoid including unnecessary sensitive personal information.

2. Professional Headline

State your professional direction or area of expertise.

Example:

Entry-Level Customer Support Professional | Communication | Customer Service

Use a headline that reflects your actual capabilities.

3. Professional Summary

Write a short summary of your relevant skills, experience and career direction.

Example for a beginner:

«Entry-level administrative professional with experience organizing information, preparing documents and supporting routine office activities. Developing proficiency in digital productivity tools, professional communication and task coordination. Seeking an opportunity to contribute to an administrative or operations team while continuing to build practical competence.»

Do not copy this summary without adapting it to your real circumstances.

4. Skills

List relevant skills that you can reasonably demonstrate.

Separate technical skills from transferable skills when doing so improves readability.

5. Experience

Include relevant employment, contract work, internships, volunteering and other legitimate experience.

Describe your actual responsibilities and contributions.

6. Projects

Include relevant projects where formal employment experience is limited.

7. Education

List relevant qualifications and institutions accurately.

8. Certifications and Training

Include relevant credentials with accurate titles and issuing organizations.

9. Additional Information

Include language proficiency, relevant professional memberships or other role-related information when appropriate.

lessons.title: 6.6.4 How to Write Strong Experience Statements
Content: «Organized incoming documents, maintained electronic records and supported the preparation of weekly administrative reports.»
The stronger statement explains the work more clearly.
Where accurate and measurable, include the result.
«Organized an electronic filing system for more than 200 records, reducing the time required to locate frequently used documents.»
Only use a number if you can substantiate it.
- Coordinated a team of four volunteers to deliver a community outreach activity.
- Prepared weekly sales reports to help management review performance.
- Resolved customer enquiries using the company's established service procedures.
- Created a spreadsheet to track project tasks and deadlines.
A beginner can describe legitimate contributions without inventing impressive metrics.

lessons.title: 6.8.1 Job Searching Is a Process
Content: An effective job search is not simply applying for every vacancy you encounter.
It is a structured process of identifying suitable opportunities, preparing targeted applications, following instructions, tracking progress and learning from outcomes.
TARGET → RESEARCH → PREPARE → APPLY → TRACK → FOLLOW UP → IMPROVE
Define the roles and industries you want to pursue.
Identify legitimate employers and relevant vacancies.
Submit the application according to instructions.
Record the application and its status.
Follow up appropriately where permitted and useful.
Review feedback and strengthen your approach.

lessons.title: 6.8.4 How to Improve Your Job Search
Content: If you are not receiving interviews, investigate:
- whether the roles match your experience;
- whether your CV clearly demonstrates relevant capabilities;
- whether your portfolio supports your claims;
- whether your job-search channels are appropriate.
If you receive interviews but no offers, investigate:
- how clearly you explain your experience;
- how well you understand the role;
- whether you communicate your strengths honestly;
- whether you demonstrate the relevant technical skills.
Do not assume every rejection means you are incapable.
Use evidence to identify what may need improvement.

Content: Use STAR to structure answers to behavioural questions.

Question: Tell us about a time you solved a problem.

Task: I was responsible for coordinating the group's task schedule.
Action: I created a shared task list, clarified individual responsibilities and introduced brief progress updates.

Use examples that actually happened. Do not invent employment stories.

Explain your interests and relevant experience.

lessons.title: 6.14.1 What Is Freelancing?
Content: Freelancing involves providing services to clients, usually through project-based, contract-based or otherwise independent arrangements.
Some forms of freelance work are regulated or require specific qualifications. Students must comply with the applicable rules.

Content: A freelancer needs more than technical competence.
Freelancers must also understand their contractual, tax and legal responsibilities.

lessons.title: 6.14.4 Avoid Freelance Scams
Content: Be cautious when an opportunity involves:
- requests for upfront recruitment fees without a credible basis;
- pressure to share passwords or security codes;
- requests to receive or transfer money on behalf of strangers;
- demands for sensitive information before legitimate verification;
- unusually high compensation for vague work;
- refusal to explain the scope of work.
Verify clients and platforms. Read contract terms. Do not pay for a job merely because someone promises employment.

lessons.title: 6.15.1 What Is a Professional Certification?
Content: A professional certification is a credential awarded under an organization's stated requirements, often involving training, assessment, experience or a combination of these.
Credentials differ in purpose and recognition.
Others require practical assessments or substantial professional experience.
A certification is not automatically a professional licence.
Certain occupations require registration, licensing or other legally specified qualifications before a person can practise.

lessons.title: 6.22 FIVE OBJECTIVE TEST QUESTIONS
Content: Select the single best answer for each question.
What is the most effective starting point when investigating a new career?
A. Purchase several certificates before researching the occupation.
B. Research the role's responsibilities, required capabilities, qualifications and available opportunities.
C. Copy the CV of a successful person in that field.
D. Apply for every vacancy with a similar job title.
Which statement best describes an effective CV?
A. It should contain every personal detail, regardless of relevance.
B. It should use complicated language to impress employers.
C. It should present accurate, relevant qualifications, skills, experience and evidence of achievements.
D. It should contain as many certificates as possible, even if they are unrelated to the role.
What does the STAR method help a candidate do?
A. Memorize the entire job description.
B. Structure a behavioural interview answer using Situation, Task, Action and Result.
C. Negotiate a higher salary without researching the role.
D. Avoid answering questions about previous experience.
Which action best demonstrates the principle of building employability?
A. Collecting certificates without practising the skills.
B. Waiting until an employer offers training before learning anything new.
C. Developing relevant skills, producing credible work samples and improving professional behaviour.
D. Applying only for positions that require no evidence of ability.
A person wants to enter data analysis but has limited practical experience. Which approach is most appropriate?
A. Claim several years of experience on the CV.
B. Purchase a certificate and assume that employment is guaranteed.
C. Research entry-level requirements, develop relevant skills, complete practical projects and pursue suitable opportunities.
D. Apply only for senior data-analysis positions.
Career research should begin with understanding the work, its requirements and the available opportunities.
An effective CV is accurate, relevant, readable and supported by credible evidence.
STAR provides a structure for explaining a real situation, responsibility, action and outcome.
Employability improves through relevant capability, practical evidence, professional behaviour and continuous development.
A realistic career transition combines research, skill development, practical evidence and targeted applications.
Recommended learning standard: A score of at least 8/10 indicates a strong initial understanding. Students scoring below 8/10 should review the relevant sections and retake the assessment.

PROJECT PART 5: PROFESSIONAL PROFILE

Prepare a professional profile suitable for LinkedIn or another relevant professional platform.

Include:

1. Headline.

2. About section.

3. Education.

4. Relevant experience.

5. Skills.

6. Projects.

7. Appropriate contact or portfolio details.

If you cannot access LinkedIn, prepare the profile as a document first.

Deliverable: A complete draft of your professional profile.

---

PROJECT PART 6: CAREER PORTFOLIO

Select one project that demonstrates a priority skill.

Examples:

- a data analysis report;

- a website;

- a business research report;

- a technical report;

- a sample customer-service procedure;

- a marketing campaign;

- a graphic-design collection;

- a project tracker;

- a sample financial spreadsheet;

- an appropriate technical project.

Your project must be relevant to your target career.

Document:

Project title: __________________

Problem addressed: __________________

Objective: __________________

Tools used: __________________

My contribution: __________________

Process followed: __________________

Result or output: __________________

What I learned: __________________

Next improvement: __________________

Deliverable: One completed work sample or a documented project plan with a realistic completion date.

Where practical work cannot be completed immediately, students must specify the next steps and schedule. The final assessment should distinguish a completed project from a proposed project.

---

PROJECT PART 7: INTERVIEW PREPARATION

Prepare written responses to five questions:

1. Tell us about yourself.

2. Why are you interested in this role?

3. What relevant skills do you possess?

4. Describe a problem you solved.

5. Why should we consider you?

Use STAR for behavioural questions where appropriate.

Then conduct a mock interview with another person or record yourself answering the questions.

Afterward, evaluate:

- clarity;

- relevance;

- honesty;

- examples;

- confidence;

- listening;

- professional conduct.

Deliverable: Five prepared answers and a mock-interview reflection.

---

PROJECT PART 8: JOB-SEARCH OR CLIENT-ACQUISITION SYSTEM

Choose the pathway most relevant to your current goal.

OPTION A: EMPLOYMENT

Identify at least five suitable opportunities.

For each, record:

- employer;

- role;

- source;

- essential requirements;

- your suitability;

- capability gaps;

- application deadline;

- next action.

If suitable vacancies are unavailable, identify target employers and establish a research plan.

OPTION B: FREELANCING

Define:

- service;

- target client;

- deliverable;

- required skills;

- portfolio evidence;

- service process;

- client acquisition channels;

- pricing considerations;

- contract and payment safeguards.

OPTION C: ENTREPRENEURSHIP

Identify:

- customer group;

- problem;

- proposed product or service;

- required capabilities;

- practical evidence;

- first customer-acquisition action;

- operating requirements.

Deliverable: One practical opportunity-access plan.

---

PROJECT PART 9: NETWORKING PLAN

Identify five people, professional communities or organizations relevant to your career.

You do not need to know all five people personally.

Create this tracker:

Person or Organization| Relevance| What I Want to Learn| Value I Can Contribute| Next Action

| | | |

| | | |

| | | |

| | | |

| | | |

Write one professional networking message.

If appropriate, send it and record the outcome. Do not misrepresent your experience or pressure people to respond.

Deliverable: Networking plan and one message.

---

PROJECT PART 10: CAREER DEVELOPMENT PLAN

Create a plan covering the next 30 days, 90 days and 12 months.

Period| Objective| Action| Evidence of Completion| Target Date

First 30 days| | | |

First 90 days| | | |

First 12 months| | | |

Your plan must include:

- a career direction;

- a skills-development objective;

- a portfolio or experience objective;

- a professional positioning objective;

- an opportunity-access objective;

- a review schedule.

---

lessons.title: 6.26 THE FOUR-TIER CAREER DEVELOPMENT ARCHITECTURE
Content: Career development should deepen as the learner advances through SGG.
The four tiers must build on one another without duplicating the same learning experience.
Who am I and how do I grow?
The learner can identify a realistic career direction, explain their value, prepare basic professional materials and follow a structured plan for developing employability.
How do I create value and produce results?
Turning capabilities into measurable economic and professional outcomes.
The learner can apply capabilities to deliver work, pursue clients or employment opportunities, demonstrate results and improve their economic contribution.
How do I lead, build and scale?
The learner can manage increasing responsibility, lead people, contribute to organizational performance and develop toward strategic leadership roles.
How do I create lasting institutional impact?
- advisory and governance responsibilities where appropriately qualified.
The learner can think beyond individual career progression and contribute to building institutions, developing leaders and creating sustainable organizational impact.

lessons.title: 6.27 IMPLEMENTATION IN THE SGG GLOBAL WEB APP
Content: The web app should make Career Development interactive.
Students complete a structured skills and interests assessment.
The system should not present a short questionnaire as a scientifically validated career diagnosis.
Students compare potential careers and record:
Students create and improve a CV using structured sections and practical guidance.
Students develop their headline, professional summary, skills and project descriptions.
Students record projects, evidence, feedback and improvements.
Students practise common questions, record answers and receive structured feedback.
AI-generated feedback should be treated as assistance rather than a guarantee of how a real employer will assess the candidate.
Students record opportunities, deadlines, application status and next actions.
The app should not claim to provide verified live vacancies unless the relevant data source and verification process are actually connected.
Students manage professional contacts, planned conversations and follow-ups.
Students submit the required documents and evidence for assessment.
Instructors should be able to review submissions, provide feedback and record results.
The purpose is to turn the web app into a career-development environment, not simply a repository of lecture notes.

lessons.title: 6.28 FINAL MESSAGE TO THE STUDENT
Content: Your career is not determined by one application, one interview, one certificate or one rejection.
It develops through decisions, learning, practical experience, relationships, opportunities and consistent improvement.
You may be starting with little experience.
You may have qualifications but no job.
You may be working in a field you want to leave.
You may already be employed but seeking advancement.
You may be building a freelance service or business.
Your starting point matters, but it does not have to define every future step.
Research the work you want to do.

A certificate may show what you studied. A CV may communicate your background. A portfolio may demonstrate your work. Your professional conduct influences how others experience working with you. Your continued development helps you adapt as your career changes.
You need to build all the relevant elements—not depend on one alone.
«“What valuable work can I learn to perform? How can I demonstrate that ability? Who needs it? How can I reach them? What must I improve to perform at a higher level?”»
That is the beginning of a more deliberate approach to career development.
Core Question: How do I identify, develop and position myself for meaningful career opportunities and sustainable professional growth?
Practical Project: My Career Development & Employability System
Completion Standard: Knowledge + Application + Evidence + Reflection + Career Development Plan
Connection to the SGG North Star

This module helps learners develop the capacity to understand themselves, create value, solve problems, build systems, work with people and produce measurable results—whether through employment, professional practice, freelancing, entrepreneurship or public service.

Also ask:

That is the beginning of a more deliberate approach to career development.
